paper_metadata.title: Quantum Reservoir Computing for Statistical Classification in a Superconducting Quantum Circuit

summary: The paper studies quantum reservoir computing in a two-mode superconducting circuit for three statistical tasks: Normal-vs-Laplace classification, Student-t inverse-degrees-of-freedom regression, and GARCH(1,1) regime classification. Reported fits show QRC is strongest in the limited-data regime, with Normal-vs-Laplace asymptotic accuracies A∞ = 0.943 ± 0.007 (QRC) versus 1.000 ± 0.005 (GLRT), Student-t RMSE scaling roughly as 0.76 T^-0.451 for QRC versus 0.93 T^-0.483 classically, and GARCH accuracies approaching 1 with classical slightly better at large T (A∞,c = 1.0000 ± 0.0013 vs A∞,q = 1.00 ± 0.13).

experiments.description: Quantum reservoir computing on a two-island superconducting circuit for Normal vs. Laplace distribution classification, evaluated against a classical generalized likelihood ratio test.

algorithm.variant: quantum reservoir computing (QRC) on a superconducting Bose-Hubbard-type reservoir
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Reservoir initialized in ground state at the start of each dataset; readout weights fit from training data

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Input data are encoded as a time-dependent gate voltage amplitude Vg driving the superconducting reservoir; no binary-variable/QUBO encoding
problem_formulation.objective_function: Classify a sequence of samples as drawn from either a Normal distribution or a Laplacian distribution, independent of location/scale parameters within the specified ranges
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Two coupled superconducting islands with Bose-Hubbard-type Hamiltonian H = sum_i [omega n_i - U/2 n_i(n_i+1) + i epsilon Vg (a_i - a_i^†)] + g12(a_1^† a_2 + a_1 a_2^†)

problem_instance.description: Binary statistical classification between Normal and Laplace-distributed samples with random parameters in fixed ranges

dataset_specification.description: mu in [1,2], sigma or b in [0.1,0.7]; training sweeps full parameter space, test parameters sampled randomly from same intervals

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Sequences of real-valued samples are fed sequentially into the reservoir; performance evaluated over independent test realizations
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Mean accuracy over independent test realizations with ±1σ error bars; scaling law fit versus sequence length T

implementation_details.noise_model: Lindblad master-equation simulation with decay channels only; no pure dephasing included
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Maximum-likelihood estimation of Normal and Laplace parameters for GLRT baseline
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Linear readout on reservoir features; accuracy computed from thresholded output

speedup_claims.factor: better at short T; classical slightly better at large T
speedup_claims.conditions: Normal vs. Laplace classification with limited data
speedup_claims.caveats: No formal asymptotic speedup; advantage is finite-sample and the classical method converges to higher asymptotic accuracy.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: No practical crossover established; classical GLRT has higher asymptotic accuracy (A∞,c = 1.000 ± 0.005 vs A∞,q = 0.943 ± 0.007).
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No demonstrated quantum resource advantage; the task is a small-scale simulated reservoir with two bosonic modes and a classical readout.
limiting_factors: No gate-based circuit or hardware execution
No formal complexity or speedup analysis

notes: hardware.type inferred as real_qpu_superconducting because the paper describes a superconducting circuit reservoir intended for real superconducting hardware, but the actual experiments are numerical simulations using QuTiP rather than a named physical device.
num_qubits not explicitly reported; the model uses two bosonic modes/islands with a bosonic cutoff nc=5 and nine measured Fock-state occupations, so a qubit register size is not directly specified.
No asymptotic complexity or formal speedup order is given; only empirical scaling with sequence length T is reported.
The paper reports QRC is competitive and better at short T, but classical GLRT wins asymptotically.
Reported fit values: QRC A∞ = 0.943 ± 0.007, classical A∞ = 1.000 ± 0.005.

experiments.description: Quantum reservoir computing on the same superconducting circuit for regression of the inverse Student-t degrees of freedom, compared with classical maximum-likelihood estimation.

algorithm.variant: quantum reservoir computing (QRC) on a superconducting Bose-Hubbard-type reservoir
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Reservoir initialized in ground state at the start of each dataset; readout weights fit from training data

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Input data are encoded as a time-dependent gate voltage amplitude Vg driving the superconducting reservoir; no binary-variable/QUBO encoding
problem_formulation.objective_function: Predict 1/nu for data drawn from a Student-t distribution with mu=0 and sigma=1
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Two coupled superconducting islands with Bose-Hubbard-type Hamiltonian H = sum_i [omega n_i - U/2 n_i(n_i+1) + i epsilon Vg (a_i - a_i^†)] + g12(a_1^† a_2 + a_1 a_2^†)

problem_instance.description: Regression task to estimate the inverse degrees of freedom of Student-t distributed samples

dataset_specification.description: mu=0, sigma=1, 1/nu swept uniformly over [1/30, 1] in training and sampled uniformly in the same range in testing

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Sequences of real-valued samples are fed sequentially into the reservoir; target is 1/nu rather than nu
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: RMSE over test predictions; mean performance over independent test realizations with ±1σ error bars; scaling law fit versus T

implementation_details.noise_model: Lindblad master-equation simulation with decay channels only; no pure dephasing included
implementation_details.classical_solver: Maximum-likelihood estimation of Student-t degrees of freedom (baseline)
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Maximum-likelihood fit of Student-t parameter nu using the raw sample sequence
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Linear readout on reservoir features; RMSE computed on 1/nu

speedup_claims.factor: lower rmse than classical across most T; similar asymptotic decay rate
speedup_claims.conditions: Student-t inverse degrees-of-freedom regression with limited to moderate sequence lengths
speedup_claims.caveats: No explicit numeric RMSE values are given in text; only fitted scaling parameters and qualitative comparison are reported.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: No practical crossover established; QRC has lower RMSE over much of the explored range, but both methods approach similar error floors at large T.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: A simulated two-mode superconducting reservoir with classical linear readout; no evidence of scalable quantum resource advantage.
limiting_factors: No asymptotic separation in the large-T limit
No complexity or resource scaling analysis

num_qubits not explicitly reported; the model uses two bosonic modes/islands with bosonic cutoff nc=5 and nine measured Fock-state occupations, so a qubit register size is not directly specified.
